div.p: Since 2023, Ecuador has faced significant challenges in the energy sector due to regional droughts impacting hydroelectric capacity and increasing reliance on energy imports. In this context, planning the expansion of the infrastructure that generates and transmits electricity to end consumers should focus on strategies that optimize the use of available resources. This paper presents a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) approach for multistage combined electricity generation and transmission planning (GTEP). The model employs a reconductoring strategy for existing 230 kV transmission lines, integrating higher-capacity conductors. The practicality and effectiveness of the model are validated through a case study of Ecuador's power system, which features a 21-bus system. The results confirm that the model provides cost-efficient solutions, with a projected investment of $4417.40 MUSD to diversify energy sources and reduce reliance on imports, a crucial step towards achieving Ecuador's energy independence by 2030.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The planning of electric system expansion faces increasingly significant challenges due to the growing energy demands in emerging and developing economies and the rapid adoption of advanced technologies with high electrical consumption in developed countries, including the expansion of electric vehicles and the integration of smart energy grids across various industrial sectors. According to the "Energy Outlook 2023", final electricity demand is projected to increase by approximately 75% by 2050 [1].

The efficiency and reliability of electrical systems are crucial for managing this increase in energy consumption. Annual costs associated with investment and operation represent only a fraction of the total costs of energy and auxiliary services traded each year. Given this, any failure in the generation or transmission system can have significant consequences for the stability of the electrical system, making it essential to have infrastructure that is not only efficient but also robust and strategically planned.

To address these challenges, planning entities utilize optimization models focused on minimizing costs, including investment, operation, and maintenance. The Generation Expansion Planning (GEP) problem addresses the identification of an investment schedule for new generation units, specifying their location and technology to meet the projected demand throughout the planning period [2]. On the other hand, Transmission Network Expansion Planning (TNEP) determines when, where, and how many new infrastructures, such as transmission lines, are necessary to meet reliability standards, economic efficiency, and sustainability [3].

Traditionally, GEP and TNEP have been treated as separate optimization problems, tackled by different market agents: producers in the case of GEP and regulated planners in the case of TNEP [4]. However, integrated planning for expanding generation and transmission (GTEP) provides significant added value, as transmission constraints can considerably influence the location and size of new generation units [5].

Research in TNEP has significantly evolved since the initial mixed integer linear disjunctive formulation proposed by Bahiense et al. [6]. The relaxation of the alternating current load flow equations presented in [7], allowed TNEP to address challenges related to reactive compensation [8], [9], security constraints [10], [11], resilience [12], distributed generation [13], and even GTEP models [14], [15]. The works of [16] and [17] tackle the TNEP problem from a different perspective, considering the repowering or reconductoring of existing transmission lines as a cost-effective alternative, given that under certain circumstances, it may be less costly to repower an existing transmission line rather than build a new circuit. For example, replacing ACSR conductors with HTLS can result in exceptional performance under a Dynamic Thermal Line Rating (DTLR) approach [18].

Although reconductoring has been discussed in the literature, to the best of the authors' knowledge, no prior studies have explored this approach for the Ecuadorian electricity system. This work develops a multistage joint generation and transmission planning model that uniquely considers the specific characteristics of Ecuador's energy mix and transmission network. The applicability of the model is demonstrated through the case study of the Ecuadorian power system, proposed as a test system (21-Bus-EC System), showcasing its potential impact and relevance to the country's electrical infrastructure.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 describes the mathematical model for generation and transmission expansion. It also outlines the data for constructing the proposed 21-Bus-EC System case study. Section 3 discusses the results obtained regarding the generation and transmission expansion strategy, along with total costs. Finally, Section 4 presents the conclusions and future research directions.

div.head: II. METHODOLOGY
div.p: This section describes the MILP model developed to cooptimize generation and transmission in the power grid, focusing specifically on reconductoring existing lines.

div.head: A. Formulation of the Problem
div.p: The problem involves optimizing the transmission network's efficiency by strategically reconductoring existing lines and integrating new generation resources where necessary. The MILP model considers the operational, construction, and upgrading costs associated with transmission and generation assets over a specified planning horizon.

1) Objective Function: The objective function, showing in Eq. ( 1), is designed to minimize the total cost of expanding and operating the transmission and generation network over a planning horizon. It incorporates the total discounted costs associated with the construction of new transmission lines cl i,j , the reconductoring of existing lines c R i,j , and the operation of generators c opg y,g , as a function of their availability and energy demand throughout the year. Additionally, the costs derived from the investment in new generators c ng and the cost of unsupplied energy c ens are considered, reflecting the economic impact of not meeting the energy demand. The costs are adjusted by a discount factor, α y , applied to each stage, reflecting the time value of money.

div.p: y,cl Ecuador's electricity system relies heavily on hydroelectricity. In 2023, of the total effective power of 8,254.45 MW, hydroelectric plants constituted 62.42%. That year, the total net energy production was 31,903.26 GWh, composed of 59.02% hydroelectricity, 26.2% thermal sources, 1.7% nonconventional renewable sources, and 8.1% imported electricity from Colombia and Peru. Additionally, 4.7% of the energy demand was not satisfied due to load-shedding protocols implemented by the system operator [19].

div.p: This strong dependence on hydroelectricity makes the system particularly vulnerable to water resource variability, exacerbated by drought scenarios linked to climate change. This vulnerability was exposed in 2023, when electricity imports from Colombia reached $285.88 MUSD, a figure ten times higher than in 2022, highlighting the critical need to diversify energy sources and strengthen the system's resilience to severe droughts [20].

The MILP model proposed in Section A will be used to investigate and address the above-mentioned challenges. The applicability of the model is illustrated by a simplified 21-node network representing the National Interconnected System of Ecuador, referred to as the 21-Bus-EC System. This network includes a 230 kV transmission ring with 15 nodes, two 138 kV nodes, and a 500 kV backbone system with four additional nodes, as shown in Figure 1. To ensure the accuracy of power flow calculations within this network, the results were validated using DigSilent PowerFactory, confirming the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed modeling approach.

The planning scenario for expanding Ecuador's electricity system extends from 2024 to 2030 maintaining a reserve margin of 15%. A multivariate linear regression model was used to determine the maximum demand to be satisfied, using GDP and population projections showing in Table I as predictor variables. The projections reveal that the demand for electric power will increase by 14.53% by the year 2030. Then, this demand is distributed among the 21 nodes according to a participation factor designated for each node as a parameter. The data used to model the thechnical and economic characteristics of the generators and loads were obtained from openaccess sources, including the Electricity Master Plan (PME) [21], reports from the electricity system operator CENACE [19], ARCERNRR [20] report and Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy Analysis report [22].

The subset of candidate generation facilities includes three hydroelectric plants as proposed in the PME: Santiago, Cardenillo, and Toachi Pilatón. Furthermore, four generic generation plants are outlined in Table II , which includes two thermal and two photovoltaic facilities strategically positioned at the Totoras, Pascuales and Santa Rosa nodes to meet the high energy demands of Ecuador's largest cities, Ambato, Guayaquil and Quito, respectively. These generation facilities are assumed to be integral components of the strategies devised by planners to mitigate the energy crisis in the short term.

To quantitatively assess the impact of climatic variations on hydroelectric generation, this study incorporates an availability factor that reflects the variability in water resources. This factor adjusts the expected output from hydroelectric facilities. It is applied to compensate for both seasonal fluctuations and long-term climatic trends, ensuring that the model accurately reflects real-world conditions. This approach is thoroughly documented in the recent academic literature, including references [23] and [24].

On the other hand, the reconductoring approach involves the replacement of existing transmission line conductors (ACSR Bluejay 1113 conductor) with higher capacity conductors (ACSS Bluejay 1113). The latter offers an ampacity 22% higher than the original conductor, as cited in [17]. This change is intended to increase the efficiency and capacity of these specific lines. Table III illustrates the lines selected for reconductoring.

The optimization model was developed using the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS) and solved with the Gurobi solver. All computational tasks were executed on a high-performance computing platform equipped with an Intel i9-13900K processor and 128 GB of RAM. To quantify the computational demands of the model, the average CPU time recorded for solving the base scenario was approximately 11.52 seconds. Table IV provides a detailed summary of the model's computational statistics.

div.head: III. RESULTS
div.p: The application of the proposed optimization model to the 21-Bus-EC System case study reveals that the budget required to address Ecuador's energy crisis through 2030 is projected to be $7169.31 MUSD. It is crucial to note that the variable costs applied in the model provide an approximation and do not necessarily reflect the exact operational reality of each power plant. Consequently, the model results are intended to provide decision support and not to define the planner's policy actions directly.

The cost breakdown for the period 2024-2030 is detailed in Table V. Investments in six new power plants account for 59.33% of the total budget. Costs associated with the operation of existing power plants represent 38.38%, underscoring the continuous need for maintaining and optimizing current assets. A smaller portion of the budget is allocated to the transmission system, including the construction of new lines and the reconductoring of existing lines, which collectively account for approximately 2.07% of the total budget. As shown in Figure 2, the 2024-2030 period underlines a sustained dependence on hydropower. By 2030, hydropower is expected to cover 72.01% of Ecuador's electricity demand. Thermal power plants are expected to contribute 25.26%, while photovoltaic generation will contribute a modest 1.75%. It is worth noting that imports from Colombia drop from 8.69% to 0.99% at the end of the planning period, indicating that even with investments in electricity generation, dependence on generation from Colombia would remain, especially in Ecuador's dry season, where availability factors tend to be lower. Although reconductoring represents a minimal cost in the total investment, the results presented in Fig. 3 suggest that increasing the transmission capacity of existing lines may result in a more cost-efficient solution.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This study presents optimal planning for the expansion of Ecuador's electrical system using a MILP model that incorporates a reconductoring approach. Key findings from the application of this model include:

The MILP model effectively integrates reconductoring strategies within a multistage planning framework for generation and transmission systems. By accounting for the comprehensive costs of construction, reconductoring, and operational dynamics, the model strategically minimizes the total cost of electricity supply over multiple planning periods.

The application of the MILP model to the 21-Bus-EC System demonstrates its utility in planning under Ecuador's heavy reliance on hydropower. The model indicates necessary investments totaling $4,253.77 MUSD for new power plants by 2030, emphasizing the shift towards diversifying energy sources. Additionally, $163.33 MUSD is allocated for enhancing the transmission system, including new constructions and reconductoring. This represents a strategic effort to reduce the system's dependence on imported electricity, which is expected to decrease to 0.99% of the energy mix by 2030.

Future research will aim to enhance the model by incorporating the stochastic nature of water resources, and climate change factors. These enhancements will allow the model to provide more comprehensive solutions that align with sustainable development goals.
